title: The transpose of a matrix
keyIdea: The transpose Aᵀ turns each row of A into a column, so an m × n matrix becomes n × m and the entry in row i, column j moves to row j, column i: (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. For a square matrix this is a reflection in the leading diagonal, which stays fixed. Transposing twice gives A back, (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ, and the transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. A matrix is symmetric when Aᵀ = A.

kid: The transpose of a matrix A is written Aᵀ. To make it, turn each row of A into a column. Row 1 becomes column 1. Row 2 becomes column 2. The numbers stay the same. Only their places change.
So the size flips. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is 2 × 3. Its transpose has 3 rows and 2 columns, so it is 3 × 2. In general an m × n matrix has an n × m transpose.

Each entry swaps its row and column number. The entry in row 2, column 3 of A goes to row 3, column 2 of Aᵀ. In symbols, (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. For a square matrix this is a mirror image in the leading diagonal. The entries on that diagonal stay put.

Two rules matter most. Transpose twice and you get A back. And the transpose of a product flips the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. A matrix is symmetric when Aᵀ = A. Then each entry below the diagonal matches its mirror above it.
adult: This topic sits in A-level Further Mathematics (pure core, matrices) and in first-year university linear algebra. The terms to use are transpose, entry, row, column, order (the m × n size), leading diagonal, square matrix, symmetric matrix and the index notation (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ.

The properties worth learning are (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A, (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ, (kA)ᵀ = kAᵀ and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. The last one follows from the index form: the (i, j) entry of (AB)ᵀ is the sum over k of aⱼₖbₖᵢ, which is the (i, j) entry of BᵀAᵀ. It also gives a quick proof that AAᵀ is always symmetric.

Common mistakes: keeping the order m × n instead of swapping it, swapping only some entries, and writing (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ. A size check catches that slip at once, since for non-square matrices AᵀBᵀ often does not exist. Another misconception is that the diagonal moves too: it is the mirror line, so it stays fixed.

In the lab your learner sends rows to columns, places single entries by swapping their indices, finds the fixed diagonal, orders Aᵀ and Bᵀ so the product equals (AB)ᵀ (the wrong order gives a 3 × 3 result) and fills the gaps of a symmetric matrix while Aᵀ updates beside it. Be careful to read every entry as row first, then column.

familyTip: Take a timetable or a league table and copy it out with the rows as columns. Ask: how many rows and columns does the new table have? Which cells stayed in the same place? Then try a times-table grid, which is symmetric: why does it look the same after the swap?

items: Aᵀ has the same order as A

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn rows into columns, swap entry indices, find the fixed diagonal, order (AB)ᵀ and build a symmetric matrix.

practice.prompt: A is a {m} × {n} matrix. How many rows does Aᵀ have?
practice.hint: The columns of A become the rows of Aᵀ.
practice.explain: A has {n} columns, and each column of A becomes a row of Aᵀ, so Aᵀ is {n} × {m} with {=n} rows.

practice.prompt: In A, the entry a₂₃ = {a}. What is the entry in row 3, column 2 of Aᵀ?
practice.hint: (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. Swap the row and column numbers.

practice.prompt: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4. What is the order of (AB)ᵀ?
practice.hint: Find the order of AB first, then swap it.
practice.explain: AB is 2 × 4, so (AB)ᵀ is 4 × 2. This matches BᵀAᵀ: 4 × 3 times 3 × 2 gives 4 × 2.

practice.prompt: Which statement is true for all matrices A and B where AB exists?
practice.hint: Check the orders with A 2 × 3 and B 3 × 4. Which product even exists?
practice.explain: The transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. With A 2 × 3 and B 3 × 4, AᵀBᵀ would be 3 × 2 times 4 × 3, which does not exist.

pool.prompt: What is the transpose of the row vector (2  5  −1)?
pool.hint: The one row becomes one column. Do the entries change order?
pool.explain: A 1 × 3 row vector transposes to a 3 × 1 column vector. The entries keep their order, 2, 5, −1, reading down the column.

pool.prompt: Which entries of a square matrix are unchanged by transposing?
choices: the entries on the leading diagonal
the entries in the first row
the entries in the last column
pool.hint: Which entries have the same row number as column number?
pool.explain: On the leading diagonal i = j, so aᵢᵢ moves to row i, column i: the same place. Every other entry reflects across that diagonal.

pool.prompt: A is symmetric and a₁₃ = {a}. What is a₃₁?
pool.hint: Symmetric means Aᵀ = A, so aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ.
pool.explain: A symmetric matrix satisfies a₃₁ = a₁₃, so a₃₁ = {=a}.

pool.prompt: A is a {m} × {n} matrix. How many entries does Aᵀ have?
pool.hint: Transposing moves entries, it does not add or remove any.
pool.explain: Aᵀ is {n} × {m}, which holds {n} × {m} = {=m*n} entries, the same as A.

pool.hint: Swap rows and columns, then swap them again.
pool.explain: The second transpose swaps every row and column back, so (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A.

pool.prompt: For any matrix A, why is AAᵀ symmetric?
choices: because every product of matrices is symmetric
pool.hint: Apply (XY)ᵀ = YᵀXᵀ with X = A and Y = Aᵀ.
pool.explain: Using the product rule, (AAᵀ)ᵀ = (Aᵀ)ᵀAᵀ = AAᵀ, so AAᵀ equals its own transpose. A need not be square, and most products are not symmetric.

pool.hint: Write row 1 of A, which is (1, 2), as column 1.
pool.explain: Row 1 (1, 2) becomes column 1 and row 2 (3, 4) becomes column 2, giving [[1, 3], [2, 4]]. The diagonal entries 1 and 4 stay put.

pool.prompt: A is 3 × {n} and B is {n} × 2. How many columns does BᵀAᵀ have?
pool.hint: Bᵀ is 2 × {n} and Aᵀ is {n} × 3. Multiply the orders.
pool.explain: Bᵀ is 2 × {n} and Aᵀ is {n} × 3, so BᵀAᵀ is 2 × 3 with 3 columns, the order of (AB)ᵀ.
